title: History in Conversation
subtitle: Historians, ideas and debates through time.

scope.geographic_emphasis: Primarily Western academic historiography, with selected independent and critical traditions.
notes: Dates describe approximate emergence or expansion, not termination.
Edges are selective teaching interpretations, not an exhaustive genealogy.
Connections may express influence, overlap, conceptual resources, or critique; read each relationship label.
A node’s source is a supporting reference and does not necessarily document every associated edge.
Nodes include traditions, fields, genres, methods, approaches, and individual thinkers.
New and revised relationships may include source_ids and evidence_note. A comparative teaching link does not assert influence merely because it has a source and target.
Editorial revision 1.3 incorporates selected and rewritten Fable 5.1 proposals into the existing revision 1.2; the supplied feedback used an older base and its edge IDs were remapped.

Schema 1.2 adds optional edge directed and relationship_kind fields. Explicit comparisons have directed:false; missing direction metadata on inherited edges means not yet classified, not verified influence. Critique arrows point from critic to the position criticized.

Optional source citation and verification fields distinguish bibliographic identity or supporting-page checks from an unperformed passage-level audit. Missing verification metadata means unrecorded, never implicitly verified. Checked metadata does not certify all node or edge interpretations.

The map remains selective: a named work, school, or field does not imply that every associated thinker agrees. Paired nodes such as Progressive/consensus history are comparisons, not single paradigms.

Revision 1.4 distinguishes women as producers of historical knowledge from women’s history as a field. Women historians appear across economic, political, military, intellectual, and other inquiries; belonging to the profession does not imply a shared feminist method or a linear succession of feminist waves.

Schema 1.3 adds shared people records, explicit group/person entry kinds, and qualified representative_people rosters. Roster inclusion is not a new influence edge or a claim of formal school membership. Most rosters normalize existing curated prose; their inherited references are not new individual affiliation verification.

Directional neighborhood views place incoming directed relationships on the left and outgoing ones on the right. Comparisons and unclassified links sit separately. Thompson’s cultural contribution and feminist historians’ productive inheritance coexist with their criticisms; no uniform succession from class to culture is implied.

From revision 1.133 the atlas has no closing date. Fields are extended one at a time; each entry states the year through which it has been reviewed. The original 1920–2000 experiment (revision 1.121) is kept as an archived view.

frame.note: Open frame from revision 1.133. Each entry records how far it has been reviewed (coverage.reviewed_through); a review year is a limit of our reading, not an ending.

chronology_policy.interpretation: A selection extent is not a lifespan, period of influence or complete field history. Unknown endpoints remain unknown. Date labels are descriptive, never instructions to the current renderer.

Preserve the 1960 event ID/date and all reading limits; add two library metadata sources. No new people, nodes, edges or dated events.

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.
